justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mildly bullish drift assumption anchored to the prevailing price level of the S&P 500 (approximated around 578–580 at the time of the forecast). For the 1-day horizon, I essentially projected very little change from the last observed price, as single-day moves in a low-volatility regime tend to cluster near zero with a slight upward bias reflecting the equity risk premium. For the 1-week estimate, I allowed for modest appreciation reflecting the historical average weekly drift of equities, while the 1-month estimate incorporates a slightly larger expected return consistent with long-run annualized equity gains of roughly 8–10%, translated into a monthly increment. None of these estimates assumed any specific catalyst; they are primarily mean-drift extrapolations from recent price levels.

The confidence interval widths are calibrated to realized and implied volatility at each horizon. For the 1-day interval, I used a daily volatility assumption of roughly 0.7–0.9%, which maps to a roughly ±14–15 point band at 90% confidence. For the 1-week horizon, volatility scales with the square root of time, widening the band to approximately ±28 points. The 1-month interval is wider still, reflecting both the longer time window and the compounding uncertainty in macro conditions, earnings releases, and Fed policy signals. Implied volatility from options markets, which was running in the low-to-mid teens on an annualized VIX basis, informed these width assumptions.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include a sudden shift in Federal Reserve communication — particularly any surprise hawkish pivot or unexpected rate cut signal — which could move the index by 2–4% in a single session, easily breaching even the 1-week interval. Geopolitical shocks, a significant miss or beat in major earnings reports from mega-cap technology companies, or an unexpected inflation or employment data print could similarly generate tail moves. On the upside, a capitulation rally driven by short covering or a positive geopolitical resolution could push the index above the upper bounds.

Finally, it is worth acknowledging that my stated intervals reflect statistical uncertainty under relatively normal market conditions and do not fully account for fat-tailed or jump-diffusion dynamics that characterize real equity markets. Historical data show that S&P 500 returns have fatter tails than a normal distribution implies, meaning true 90% intervals should arguably be somewhat wider than what standard volatility-scaling produces. If market liquidity were to deteriorate sharply, or if correlations across asset classes broke down in a stress scenario, all three intervals could be violated simultaneously in the same direction.
